title: Pressure in gases — particles in motion
examTip: Gas pressure questions almost always want an explanation using particles. Say 'more frequent collisions with the container walls', not just 'particles move faster'. And always check that a Boyle's Law question is at constant temperature.
introTips: Pressure is caused by gas particles hitting the walls of their container. More hits, or harder hits, means higher pressure.
Temperature is really a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles. Hotter means faster.
The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero (0 K = −273 °C). You must convert to Kelvin before using any gas law equation.
Boyle's Law only works at constant temperature. If the temperature changes, use the combined gas law instead.
p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ and pV/T = constant are the two equations you need. Know them and be able to use them.
intro: You see gas pressure at work when you pump up a bike tyre. You see it when you squeeze a balloon. You see it when a weather balloon grows as it rises. Gas pressure is not a mysterious force. It is simply billions of tiny particles crashing into a container's walls, again and again. Understanding this is powerful. You can predict exactly what happens to the pressure when you heat a gas. You can also predict what happens when you squash it into a smaller space. Engineers use these ideas to design car engines, aerosol cans and scuba diving equipment.

keyPoints.heading: What causes gas pressure
keyPoints.content: Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container. Each collision pushes on the wall with a tiny force. Huge numbers of particles collide every second. So the total effect is a steady pressure that you can measure. Pressure = force ÷ area. So more collisions per second, or harder collisions, means higher pressure. Key idea: the faster the particles move, the harder and more frequently they hit the walls → higher pressure. If you heat the gas, particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often → pressure rises (if the volume is fixed). Now squash the gas into a smaller volume. The same number of particles are in a smaller space. They hit the walls more often per second → pressure rises (if the temperature is fixed).
writeBullets: Gas pressure — caused by gas particles colliding with the container walls
Each collision pushes with a force. Billions of collisions per second make a pressure you can measure
Higher temperature → faster particles → harder, more frequent collisions with the walls → higher pressure
Smaller volume → same particles in less space → more frequent collisions with the walls → higher pressure
Pressure = force ÷ area (Pa = N/m²)

keyTerms.def: The force per unit area exerted by gas particles colliding with container walls
A particle striking the container wall — each collision exerts a tiny force contributing to total pressure

keyPoints.memTip: More collisions OR harder collisions = higher pressure. Temperature controls speed. Volume controls how often they hit.
keyPoints.tutor_note: You need to link the cause (particle collisions) to the effect (pressure) clearly. Mark schemes reward the phrase 'collisions with the walls'.

keyPoints.heading: Absolute zero and the Kelvin scale
keyPoints.content: In physics, temperature is measured in Kelvin (K), not just Celsius. The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero: 0 K = −273 °C. At absolute zero, particles have the least kinetic energy possible. In theory, they stop moving completely. This is the lowest possible temperature. You cannot go below it. To convert: T (K) = θ (°C) + 273. Examples: 0 °C = 273 K; 100 °C = 373 K; 20 °C = 293 K; −73 °C = 200 K. You must always use Kelvin in gas law calculations. Using Celsius gives completely wrong answers. The equations need a scale that starts at absolute zero. The Kelvin scale matters for another reason. At 0 K the pressure would be zero. Particles would have no kinetic energy and make no collisions. This has a real physical meaning, which 0 °C does not.
writeBullets: Absolute zero — 0 K = −273 °C. The lowest possible temperature
At absolute zero, particles have the least kinetic energy. In theory, they stop moving
Kelvin conversion: T (K) = θ (°C) + 273
Always use Kelvin in gas law equations. Celsius gives wrong answers

keyTerms.def: The lowest possible temperature: 0 K = −273 °C; particles have minimum kinetic energy
The absolute temperature scale; T(K) = θ(°C) + 273; must be used in gas law equations

keyPoints.memTip: Add 273 to convert °C to K. Take away 273 to go back. 0 K = absolute zero = −273 °C.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A very common mistake is leaving temperature in °C in gas law calculations. Always convert first.

keyPoints.heading: Boyle's Law — pressure and volume at constant temperature
keyPoints.content: Take a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. Its pressure and volume are inversely proportional. So p × V = constant, or p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. If you halve the volume, the pressure doubles. If you double the volume, the pressure halves. Particle explanation: squash the gas into half the volume. The same number of particles now have less space. They hit the walls twice as often per second → pressure doubles. Units: pressure in Pa (pascals) or kPa. Volume in m³ or cm³. Both sides must use the same unit. Worked example: a gas has pressure 200 kPa and volume 3 m³. It is squashed to 1.5 m³ at constant temperature. Find the new pressure: p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = (200 × 3) ÷ 1.5 = 600 ÷ 1.5 = 400 kPa.
writeBullets: Boyle's Law: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ at constant temperature
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional. When one doubles, the other halves
Halve the volume → particles hit walls twice as often → pressure doubles
Units: pressure in Pa or kPa. Volume in m³ or cm³. Use the same units on both sides
Rearrange: p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ or V₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ p₂

keyTerms.def: At constant temperature, p × V = constant for a fixed mass of gas; p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
When one quantity doubles, the other halves — their product stays constant

keyPoints.memTip: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. Both sides equal the same constant.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Check that the temperature is stated as constant before you use Boyle's Law. If the temperature changes, you need the combined law.

keyPoints.heading: The combined gas law — pressure, volume and temperature
keyPoints.content: When the temperature can change too, use the combined gas law. It is p₁V₁ / T₁ = p₂V₂ / T₂, where T is in Kelvin. It joins two laws. Boyle's Law links p and V at constant T. Gay-Lussac's Law links p and T at constant V. If the volume is fixed, as in a rigid container: p/T = constant. So doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles the pressure. Particle explanation: at a higher temperature, particles move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often → pressure rises. Worked example: a gas is at 100 kPa, 2 m³ and 300 K. It is heated to 600 K at constant volume. New pressure: p₂ = p₁ × T₂ / T₁ = 100 × 600/300 = 200 kPa. Always convert °C to K before substituting. This is the most common mistake in exam answers.
writeBullets: Combined gas law: p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ (T must be in Kelvin)
Fixed volume: p/T = constant. Doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles the pressure
Higher temperature → faster particles → harder, more frequent collisions → higher pressure
Always convert temperature to Kelvin before substituting into any gas law
Rearrange for any unknown: p₂ = p₁V₁T₂ / (T₁V₂)

keyTerms.def: p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂; links pressure, volume and temperature for a fixed mass of gas
At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature: p/T = constant

keyPoints.memTip: pV/T = constant. Each fraction equals the same number.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Write out T in Kelvin before you substitute. It stops the most common calculation mistake.

0.question: A gas is heated in a sealed, rigid container. Why does its pressure rise?
options: The particles move faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often
The particles get bigger and push on the walls
The particles slow down and stick to the walls
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Faster particles hit the walls harder and more often. So the force on the walls goes up, and so does the pressure.
0.wrongFeedback: Heating does not change the number or size of the particles. It makes them move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises.

2.question: A sealed container of gas has a pressure of 150 kPa at a volume of 4 m³. The gas is squashed to 2 m³ at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
2.correctFeedback: Correct! p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ → p₂ = (150 × 4) ÷ 2 = 300 kPa. Halving the volume doubles the pressure.
2.wrongFeedback: Use Boyle's Law: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. Rearrange: p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = (150 × 4) ÷ 2 = 300 kPa. When volume halves, pressure doubles.

1.question: What is 27 °C converted to Kelvin?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! T(K) = θ(°C) + 273 = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Always convert to Kelvin before using gas law equations.
1.wrongFeedback: Convert using T(K) = θ(°C) + 273 = 27 + 273 = 300 K. You must add 273. Don't use the Celsius value directly.

3.question: A gas in a container with a fixed volume is at 200 kPa and 300 K. It is heated to 450 K. What is the new pressure?
3.correctFeedback: Correct! At fixed volume, p/T = constant: p₂ = p₁ × T₂/T₁ = 200 × 450/300 = 300 kPa.
3.wrongFeedback: At fixed volume, p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂. So p₂ = p₁ × T₂/T₁ = 200 × (450/300) = 300 kPa. Temperature must be in Kelvin.

commonMistakes: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin in gas law equations. Always convert first: T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.
Using Boyle's Law when the temperature also changes. Boyle's Law only works at constant temperature. If T changes, use pV/T = constant.
Giving a vague reason for a pressure rise, like 'particles move faster'. You must say 'more frequent or harder collisions with the walls' for full marks.
Mixing units in an equation. Pressure must be in the same units on each side: both Pa or both kPa. The same goes for volume.
Saying pressure goes up when volume goes up. It is the opposite. Bigger volume → particles hit the walls less often → pressure falls.
examTips: Always convert temperature to Kelvin (add 273) before substituting into any gas law. This mistake loses the most marks.
Particle explanations must mention collisions with the container walls, not just particle speed. You need both parts for full marks.
For Boyle's Law answers, check: does the pressure go up when the volume goes down? If yes, your answer makes sense.
Say which law you are using and write out the equation before substituting. This gets method marks, even if you make a maths slip.
revisionCardBullets: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the container walls
Higher temperature → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure
Smaller volume → more frequent collisions per unit area → higher pressure
Absolute zero: 0 K = −273 °C. The lowest possible temperature
Volume halves → pressure doubles (at constant temperature)
Combined gas law: p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ (T in Kelvin)
Fixed volume: p/T = constant. Doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles the pressure
Pressure units: Pa (pascals). Volume units: m³ or cm³. Keep them the same on both sides
